uncited: **Brick Data:** A contiguous memory block for each brick.
**Subdivision:** Divide the global volume into a 3D grid of bricks.
**Overlap Generation:** Duplicate voxels from neighboring bricks into the current brick's boundary layers to support interpolation.
**Sorting:** Calculate the distance from the camera/observer to the center of each brick.
*   Apply a texture matrix transformation to map the brick's local coordinates to the global view space.
*   **Boundary Artifacts:** Naive subdivision causes interpolation errors at brick boundaries because texture units lack neighbor information.
*   **Double Counting:** If a ray exits exactly on a border, samples may be blended twice.
*   **Performance Bottleneck:** CPU-GPU transfer speed is the primary bottleneck.
*   **Memory Management:** Sending a texture to the GPU creates a copy in RAM on some architectures (e.g., older NVIDIA Quadro).
Introduced by Weiskopf et al. (2004), this approach reorganizes bricks into different orientations to average out performance variations from viewing angles.

It distributes work across 64-thread blocks, assigning each thread an x-coordinate to ensure memory coalescing.
*   **Time Complexity:** Rendering time is dominated by the number of bricks $N_b$ and the transfer time $T_{transfer}$.

*   **When Not to Use:** When the volume fits entirely in GPU memory (use direct 3D textures); when compression is required (use [Brick-based Volume Rendering with Packed Textures](7106-brick-based-volume-rendering-with-packed-textures.md)); when dynamic updates are frequent and I/O is the bottleneck (use [Dynamic Rebricking](2823-dynamic-rebricking.md)).
